title: The Normal law and the central limit theorem
dek: A Normal is a two-parameter location-scale density. The CLT says that many sample means become approximately Normal. It does not say that your raw CFU values were Gaussian.
story: The Normal (Gaussian) family is indexed by a mean μ and a variance σ² > 0. The density is the familiar bell: proportional to exp{−(y−μ)²/(2σ²)}. Standard Normal means μ = 0, σ = 1; any other Normal is a location-scale shift, Z = (Y − μ)/σ ~ N(0,1). Linear combinations of independent Normals are Normal. That closure is why linear models like this family.

The central limit theorem is a different claim: if Y₁, …, Yₙ are iid with finite mean μ and finite variance σ², then √n (Ȳ_n − μ)/σ →d N(0,1). The Yᵢ need not be Normal. The theorem is about the sampling law of the mean (and, with more work, of many other smooth estimators). A histogram of n = 12 MICs can still look nothing like a bell.

In a TB lab the CLT is why a Wald interval for a proportion or a log-rate can be a first approximation, and why it is a bad last approximation when nπ is 3, when a cluster variance dominates, or when the functional is a maximum rather than a mean. Name the finite-n object you actually computed.
deepTitle: What is Normal, what is only approximately, what is not
deep: 68–95–99.7 is a Normal mnemonic for 1, 2, 3 σ. Chebyshev only gives 1/k². If you need 0.003 outside 3σ, you assumed a shape.
Law of large numbers: Ȳ_n →p μ. That is consistency of the mean, not a Normal shape. The CLT is the next-order fluctuation, order 1/√n.
Delta method: a smooth g(Ȳ) inherits a Normal limit with variance (g′(μ))² σ²/n. Logits, log-rates, and back-transformed CFU intervals live here (own plate).

Sums of independent Normals: if Yⱼ ~ N(μⱼ, σⱼ²) independent, ∑ Yⱼ ~ N(∑ μⱼ, ∑ σⱼ²). χ²_k is the law of a sum of k independent standard Normal squares. t uses a Normal numerator over an independent χ²-based denominator. Those named laws are why software prints t and χ², not because the genes are Gaussian.

Failure modes: heavy tails (no finite variance, CLT may fail), dependence (you need a different n_eff), and rare events (skewed binomial, Poisson). QQ plots (own plate) are a display of this assumption, not a ritual blessing.

formulas.label: Classical CLT
formulas.note: iid, finite variance. The Yᵢ need not be Normal.

formulas.label: Wald interval for a mean
formulas.note: Plug-in Normal approximation for Ȳ. Fragile for small n or heavy tails.

visual.caption: Three laws on the scale of a sample mean: a skewed parent (schematic), the tighter sampling law of Ȳ at moderate n, and the Normal approximation sitting on that mean. The CLT is the last curve being a usable stand-in for the middle one — not a claim about the parent.

example.title: Proportion with n = 50 versus n = 8
example.setup: π̂ from iid Bernoulli. First: 8/50. Second: 1/8. Both have the same point estimate 0.16. People quote π̂ ± 1.96 √(π̂(1−π̂)/n) both times.

steps.title: n = 50
steps.body: se ≈ √(0.16×0.84/50) ≈ 0.052. The 1.96 se interval is about 0.06 to 0.26. nπ̂ = 8 is a bit thin for Wald theatre, but the Normal approximation is at least discussing a mean of 50 bounded indicators.

steps.title: n = 8
steps.body: se ≈ √(0.16×0.84/8) ≈ 0.13. The same recipe gives an interval that comes close to 0 and is still a Normal tail on a highly skewed binomial. A score or exact interval is the adult object.

steps.title: What the CLT promised
steps.body: The theorem promised a limit for Ȳ, not a licence to treat one success in eight as a Gaussian likelihood. If you need a number for n = 8, write a binomial likelihood or a Beta posterior, not a z.

example.takeaway: The CLT is about means in growing n. Rare events and tiny n keep their skew.

check.prompt: The classical CLT is a statement about:
choices: The histogram of the raw observations Yᵢ always looking bell-shaped for n > 30
The sampling law of Ȳ_n (and similar means) becoming approximately Normal as n grows, given finite variance
check.answer: The sampling law of Ȳ_n (and similar means) becoming approximately Normal as n grows, given finite variance
check.why: The Yᵢ need not be Normal. The mean’s sampling law is the object that Gaussianises.

whyWrong.The histogram of the raw observations Yᵢ: n > 30 is folklore; the parent can stay skewed.
whyWrong.Independence being unnecessary: The classical statement uses iid (or weak dependence with a different proof).
whyWrong.Variance becoming infinite: The classical CLT needs finite variance.

check.prompt: iid observations with s = 10, n = 25. The usual Normal-approximation SE for Ȳ is:
check.why: s/√n = 10/5 = 2. The SD of one Y is 10; the SE of the mean divides by √n.

whyWrong.10: That is s, the estimated SD of Y, not of Ȳ.
whyWrong.0.4: That is 10/25, dividing by n instead of √n.

check.prompt: On the density plate, the Normal curve is drawn next to the sampling law of Ȳ in order to show:
check.figureHint: Three curves: skewed parent, Ȳ, Normal stand-in.
choices: That the parent Y must be Gaussian before you may compute Ȳ
That the CLT approximates the law of the mean, not the parent
That variance of Ȳ grows with n
That χ² is the parent of Y
check.answer: That the CLT approximates the law of the mean, not the parent
check.why: The parent stays skewed in the picture. The approximation target is Ȳ.

whyWrong.That the parent Y must be Gaussian befor: You may always compute Ȳ; Gaussianity is an extra claim.
whyWrong.That χ² is the parent of Y: χ² is a different named law (sum of Normal squares).
